Abstract: Intellectual contribution: Arctic coastal communities are part of a linked socioecological system consisting of the environment, the communities, and the social institutions developed to sustain the system. Co-management institutions able to link traditional knowledge and real-time observations of environmental change to local, regional and national institutions charged with managing marine resources are theorized to be a source of system resilience in the face of rapid change. Many researchers have investigated the role of community self-organization in the success of co-management institutions but few have studied federal agency capacities to engage in the same institutional processes. The proposed study examines to what extent agency culture, structure and history affects federal agencies’ capacities for successful co-management. The study compares two federal agencies, the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service, in their implementation of the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA) of 1972. Despite being guided by the same federal policy, the agencies’ implementation and active involvement in co-management has been different in terms of how they create collaborative agreements, for what purposes, and the structure of forums for interaction between staff and user communities; thus, these two agencies provide a unique basis for an examination of institutional performance in a time of rapid Arctic change. Empirical evidence based on four case studies of co-management regime performance for the management of polar bear, walrus, bowhead whales and beluga whales will be analyzed through the theoretical lenses of institutional analysis and resilience. Most empirical work to date on co-management has focused on the Canadian North; a significant contribution of this project is its focus on government’s role in comanagement in the Alaskan context.    Broader Impacts: This study has several aspects of broad impact to the marine mammal management policy community, user communities, and Alaska Native peoples. The study will identify the unique benefits that local communities and traditional knowledge holders bring to co-management of marine mammal resources as well as investigate how state and federal agency cooperation is shaped by both internal and external forces. The research program will be closely coordinated with the co-management organizations involved as case studies, with the project’s results disseminated to those boards, the umbrella organization representing marine mammal subsistence users, and the federal agencies involved. In this way, the project will provide a process of self-evaluation by those involved in these co-management processes and others interested in institutionalizing them in other settings. This work could also be useful during future Congressional reauthorization hearings related to co-management provisions in the MMPA. The marine mammal co-management policy community in Alaska is unique in that Alaska Native women hold many positions of power within the management organizations. The investigator intends to solicit subsistence management and ecological history from women as well as all other sectors of the communities involved, in order to gain the broadest understanding of subsistence in each case. Finally, the student investigator intends to hire a local assistant for the study and include presentations to schools in Barrow and other communities visited during the course of the research.
Project_Title: Doctoral Dissertation Research: The effect of agency culture on institutional performance: a comparative study of marine mammal co-management regimes in Alaska

Abstract: This collaborative effort (0612527, Hutchings; 0611991, Geiger; 0612105, Kambhamettu) is a joint field-remote sensing-modelling campaign to investigate the dynamic component of sea ice mass balance. The field campaign will occur over a 2-month period in spring 2007, at the planned U.S. Navy ice camp. As it happens, the season and location of the camp occurs when the dynamic component dominates the mass balance, through the formation of leads and ridging in an ice cover that is nearing its maximum annual mean thickness.     Data collected will be used to directly validate model parameterizations of the stress-strain rate relationship and mechanical redistribution. We will test model configurations commonly used in Global Climate Models (GCMs), to provide the GCM community with a direct estimate of how accurately such models reproduce the ridging and dynamic-thermodynamic control of the thickness distribution. A series of model runs will be performed to estimate sea ice mass sensitivity to model parameters and variables. Combined analysis of this model output, observations and sensor inter-comparisons will allow us to identify key monitoring requirements to compliment model uncertainties. These results will be provided to SEARCH and other relevant planning communities for Arctic Ocean Observing System design.    The project addresses key research needs consistently identified in recent program documents generated as part of SIMBA, SEARCH, DAMOCLES, IPY, and ACIA. It builds upon our most recent understanding of sea ice dynamics, derived from previous field campaigns, including AIDJEX, SIMI, SHEBA, and Beaufort Sea 2002. A major end product is a comprehensive data set with which to validate and improve dynamic-thermodynamic sea ice models.
Project_Title: Collaborative Research: Detailed Investigation of the Dynamic Component of Sea Ice Mass Balance

Abstract: In spite of its role in the geological, ecological, engineering, and climate change sciences, modeling of permafrost has remained the domain of individuals and small groups of scientists and hence little direct interaction between the permafrost and climate modeling community has  taken place. The research proposed here seeks to bridge this gap at the local to regional scale for two quite different geographical regions: western Greenland and Alaska. More specifically, climate modeling will be performed at an unprecedented spatial scale that allows us to address  central permafrost issues such as the accurate delineation of different zones of permafrost, active layer depth and seasonality, thereby combining climate modeling with spatially oriented approaches to permafrost modeling at scales of societal interest. The project will incorporate existing near-surface weather, climate and permafrost observations supplemented with new targeted measurements at locations where climate change is presently taking place, e.g. in the discontinuous permafrost zone. The following are the project’s main objectives:  • The provision of regional climate simulations for the present and future at unprecedented spatial resolution for two very distinct areas of permafrost: western Greenland (a coastal/maritime permafrost regime) and northern Alaska (a continental interior permafrost regime) using a thoroughly validated regional climate model for the Arctic;  • Establishment of a series of permafrost and climate monitoring sites representative of the range of permafrost types encountered near the permafrost margin of the two regions;   • Implementation of a state-of-the art permafrost model to be calibrated against field measurements and to be driven by the output of the regional climate model;  • A quantitative assessment of how permafrost responds to these climate change simulations using state-of-the-art permafrost models, which will permit mapping of the permafrost conditions for the present and future;  • An evaluation of the implications in the context of planning as well as mitigation and adaptation to climate change in Greenland and Alaska;  • A demonstration of the added value of this high-resolution modeling approach for Greenland and Alaska, given the significant differences in geography, climatology and infrastructure.  • The project will work out Risk Maps that will be of practical use to technical institutions and the public.  Of these objectives, the first four represent the project’s main scientific thrusts, while the latter three represent broader impacts and outreach to the non-science as well as to the scientific community.
Place: Gakona, Ilulissat, Kangerlussuaq, Nuuk, Prudhoe Bay, Qaanaaq, Sisimiut, Toolik
Project_Title: Recent and future permafrost variability, retreat and degradation in Greenland and Alaska: An integrated approach

Abstract: The arctic terrestrial landscape is undergoing structural changes that appear to be the result of climate warming and altered precipitation regimes, including shrub expansion within portions of arctic Alaska. These vegetation changes may have local to global consequences, including shifts in the albedo-climate feedback, altered animal abundances, and changes in carbon and nitrogen cycling. Once established, shrubs may subsequently alter the tundra surface roughness, leading to increased snow depth. Deeper snow provides greater physical protection of shrub meristems and branches and results in warmer winter soil temperatures setting the stage for a feed-forward cycle of continued shrub encroachment. We have an initial set of postulates regarding the environmental triggers, controls and feedbacks of shrub increases, but a mechanistic and detailed perspective is now required to reach the next intellectual platform of understanding. We have found that one potential trigger of vegetation  changes is increases in snow depth, as reported for our long-term (12-year) experiment at Toolik Lake, AK. Transforming our understanding of vegetation change in the arctic now requires a detailed mechanistic investigation of how shrubs come to dominate in response to snow depth increases.  We will quantify how increases in shrubs have altered the abiotic environment and caused a fundamental change in the functional attributes of these systems in arctic Alaska. Our studies are needed immediately as warming is progressing at an unprecedented rate in Alaska. Land managers, policy makers and scientists must understand changes in the structure and function of ecosystems in arctic Alaska, if informed land use decisions are to be made and if accurate predictions are to be presented by forecasting models. Our project is designed to contribute to the International Polar Year and its articulation of the “State of the Arctic”, and the IPY specific research themes of Tundra Experiments, Cold Land Processes, and Climate Changes in Alaska The goals of this project and the focus of our intellectual merit are thus: a) quantify how shrub increases affect the year-long temperature and water regimes of arctic tundra, quantify how shrub increases change the energy balance of the system and how these changes in vegetation community attributes may feedback to climate; b) delineate the processes controlling shrub increases, especially soil and plant N mineral nutrition and the physical protection of shrub meristems and branches by deeper snow; and c) quantify how shrub density increases have affected the patterns and magnitudes of carbon cycling (C gain, C loss and C allocation), water relations and growth above and belowground. The broader implications of our project will be highlighted by: a) the development of a CD targeted to high school science classes, that will address climate change in the arctic and the processes governing shrub encroachment across northern landscapes; b) the organization of a special session at the American Geophysical Union (AGU) that will address structural and functional changes in the arctic associated with changes in winter conditions, woody plant increases and feedback consequences to climate, and c) fully integrate our undergraduate students into the research process by having them participate in the UAA Undergraduate Research and Scholarship Program (see  http://www.uaa.alaska.edu/ours). Our research is essential today because understanding the mechanisms and the consequences of shrub encroachment are central to deciphering the controls on structural and functional changes in the arctic. Our lack of understanding is manifested by our inability to explain the sporadic nature of shrub encroachment across northern Alaska. Using the only long-term snow manipulation experiment in the foothills of arctic Alaska, we will leverage previous research investments and provide a legacy database for IPY. Should other  colleagues received funding for their winter precipitation manipulation experiments in Greenland, Sweden, Norway and Canada, our project will then contribute to a synoptic pan arctic understanding of arctic vegetation change, mechanisms and feedbacks.
Project_Title: Mechanisms and feedback consequences of shrub expansion following long-term increases in winter snow depth in northern Alaska: a legacy for IPY

Abstract: The proposed work will test the hypothesis that melting ice is a significant source of Fe for biological growth in the stratified Bering Sea shelf water during spring. The initial algal growth in spring depletes available Fe in the winter-mixed surface water, resulting in a Fe limitation of algal growth. The Fe input from melting ice relieves this Fe limitation and supports a high level of dissolved Fe in the stratified shelf surface water for subsequent algal growth when macronutrients are transported inshore from the Fe-poor but macronutrient-rich waters of the Aleutian basin. To test this hypothesis, the proposed work which will be conducted on Bering Sea Ecosystem Studies (BEST) cruises in year 2008 will investigate whether Fe in the water immediately beneath sea ice cover is depleted before macronutrients are depleted during the initial algal growth in spring in the absence of available Fe input from melting sea ice, and will examine whether melting sea ice is an important source of available Fe that leads to a persistent excess of Fe in the stratified ice-free shelf surface water.    The concentration of total dissolved Fe, total weak acid dissolvable Fe and macronutrients in surface water immediately beneath the winter ice cover will be determined during early spring in the eastern Bering Sea shelf and shelf break; on-deck bottle incubation experiments will be performed using waters from immediately beneath the winter ice cover to determine if Fe is depleted before macronutrients at enhanced sun irradiance; the concentration of dissolved Fe and total weak acid dissolvable Fe in floating ice and ice cores will be measured to quantify potential Fe input flux from melting ice; and the concentration of total dissolved Fe, total weak acid dissolvable Fe, and dissolved Fe-binding organic ligands in the shelf surface water will be determined during and after ice melting to understand how ice derived Fe influences surface water Fe concentration with time. Previously developed and tested methods will be used for clean sample collection and Fe analysis, and to process ice cores for Fe analysis.      This proposal is a stand-alone project that will benefit from and complement other projects proposed for the BEST program that seek to understand how changes in ice dynamics caused by climate change influence the Bering Sea ecosystem.  The project involves graduate students and undergraduates from the University of Alaska Fairbanks (UAF), an EPSCoR institution and  has relevance for a broad constituency of Native communities, itinerant commercial fishing and shipping communities, resource managers and policy makers throughout the Arctic and the North Pacific Ocean.
Project_Title:
BEST: The Role of Ice Melting in Providing Available Iron to the
Surface Water of the Eastern Bering Sea Shelf

Abstract: Researchers on this collaborative project will investigate the importance of halogen chemistry in OH and HO2 radical production and loss above sunlit snow, and identify significant halogen sources and transport mechanisms to this unique and remote environment. Methods: They will integrate a set of field measurements focused on the impact of halogen chemistry on the production and fate of free radicals in the Summit, Greenland surface layer. They plan to make the first measurements of BrO in the boundary layer at Summit. In addition to direct measurements of HOx, the radical precursors and sinks thought to play an important role in the OH budget in this environment (O3, NO, NO2, H2O, HONO, RONO2, HCHO, HCOOH, CH3COOH, CO, CH4, and reactive NMHCs) will be measured, as well as a number of halogen species (BrO, IO, OIO, and soluble gas phase bromide).     Measurements of various mercury species and NMHC oxidation products will provide additional evidence of reactive halogens. Rates of photochemical reactions will be measured above and within the snow. Measurements over a wide range of environmental (e.g., temperature, light, wind speed) conditions as well as a variety of transport regimes will help to discriminate the relative importance of halogens on HOx photochemical cycling. Field measurements will be interpreted with the aid of state-of-the-art back-trajectory tools (FLEXPART) and by employing a photochemical steady-state box-model to determine the HOx cycling within the Summit boundary layer. An advanced 1D multiphase chemical transport model (MISTRA) allows the assessment of the researchers’ understanding of HOx/halogen interactions, the discrimination of the proposed halogen sources, as well as allowing the extrapolation of their observations to other snow covered regions.    Broader impacts: With only a handful of HOx measurements in snow covered regions to date, lack of understanding of HOx photochemical cycling is not surprising. If halogens play a role in the HOx cycling at Summit, atmospheric modelers will need to adjust their chemical mechanisms accordingly. This project provides an unusual opportunity for graduate and undergraduate students to participate in ground-breaking science. The researchers place a high priority on conveying their excitement and the significance of the program to students and the public through web pages tracking field campaigns and via outreach presentations in local schools. Direct teacher participation will ensure the development of materials suitable for dissemination and use in schools nationwide. The team will work with news media - including radio, newspapers, and television - to provide broad public exposure.
Project_Title:
Collaborative Research: Radical Chemistry over Sunlit Snow:
Interactions between HOx and Halogen Chemistry at Summit, Greenland

Abstract: Arctic plants are strongly limited by low levels of available nitrogen yet organic N in the soil is abundant. To aid in obtaining nitrogen and other nutrients, woody plants such as Salix, Betula, Vaccinium, and Ledum form symbioses with mycorrhizal fungi. In this symbiosis, fungi obtain inorganic and organic N from soil N pools and transfer organic N compounds to plants while obtaining sugars from plants. Research into these pathways until now was either qualitative or relied on added 15N-organic compounds at artificially high concentrations, making extrapolation to natural ecosystems difficult. Now, recent research in tussock tundra at Toolik Lake, Alaska uses natural levels of 15N to quantify the amount of N supplied to plants by the symbiosis as well as the amount of carbon moving from the plants to fungi (Hobbie and Hobbie in press). At Toolik Lake, a mass balance of the natural abundance of 15N in soil, in ectomycorrhizal (ECM) fungi, and in ECM and ericoid mycorrhizal plants was used to calculate that 60-90% of the N in these plants entered via the fungi. The calculation was then extended to conclude that 8-17% of carbon fixed in photosynthesis goes to  symbiotic fungi. A second new method determines directly the presence of soil-derived organic N in plant and fungal tissues by natural radiocarbon (14C) measurements on protein vs. structural C. Implications for Arctic research on C and N cycling include the following: 1) to understand  current N cycling and predict N cycling under future climates, information is needed on what controls mycorrhizal growth and whether these fungi can access nitrogen locked in soil organic matter; 2) models of pan-Arctic C cycling must be modified to include the energy cost to plants of  mycorrhizal growth and the accompanying supply of nitrogen to woody plants by mycorrhizal fungi. The research has several goals:  1. Apply the 15N method to different types of tundra at Toolik Lake and Abisko Sweden to estimate C and N cycling through the mycorrhizal symbiosis. Intensive sampling of 15N variability will be carried out at Toolik Lake on plants, soils, and ECM fruiting bodies in tussock, heath, and shrubby tundra, with additional sampling along a north-south transect in Alaska. 2. Use long-term experiments on effects of warming and fertilization at Toolik Lake and Abisko (Sweden) to estimate how soil warming and increased nutrient availability will affect soil biomass (i.e., ergosterol) of mycorrhizal fungi and the 15N content in soils, plants, and mycorrhizal fungi. 3. Test the hypothesis that organic N molecules in Arctic soils are transmitted from the soil directly to mycorrhizal plants and fungi rather than first being mineralized to inorganic N. The 14C natural abundance in chitin, amino acids and proteins in soil and in protein and structural C of plants and mycorrhizal fungi will be measured to determine if C is coming from old soil C or recent sugars. Broader impacts resulting from the proposed activity include training of graduate (UNH) and undergraduate (summer research, Colorado College) students. K-12 students at Barrow (predominately Inupiat Eskimo) will learn about the project and assist in collecting mushrooms and plants through the Barrow Schoolyard program, funded in part by the Arctic LTER project. This research project will set up a partnership between an undergraduate institution and two research institutions. The research findings will create a paradigm shift -- forest and ecosystem scientists must now take into consideration the mycorrhizal symbionts and their role in supplying organic nitrogen from soil to shrubs and trees. Research emphasis will refocus to study the fungal abilities to attack soil organic matter. New measurements must be made of the effects of increased CO2 concentrations and a warming climate on below-ground N cycling and allocation to fungal symbionts. Because this study will provide methods to assess the importance of both C allocation to mycorrhizal fungi and organic N uptake in ecosystems, it will facilitate the inclusion of these important processes in ecosystem C and N models used for management. The high purity preparatory liquid chromatographic separation with MS detection of amino acids, proteins and chitin after chemical fractionation also introduces new methodology that may be broadly used.
Project_Title: Collaborative Research: Most Arctic Plants Obtain Nitrogen by Symbiosis with Fungi: Development of a Radical Concept Cooperative Project

Abstract: This proposal requests support for interdisciplinary research activities to be carried out in association with a pilot field experiment planned for the northern-hemisphere summer season of 2006 at Helheim Glacier, East Greenland. The main goal of the proposed study is to obtain an understanding of the mechanisms by which glacial earthquakes are generated, and of their relation to glaciological and climatological processes.  A new class of earthquakes occurring at glaciers in Alaska, Antarctica, and Greenland was identified in 2003 by Ekstr¨om et al. (2003). Teleseismic analysis indicates that these glacial earthquakes are the result of rapid sliding of the glacial ice over the glacier bed; during each sliding episode,  a 10-km3 volume of ice may slide as far as 10 m during a period of 30–60 s. Little is understood about the mechanism by which glacial earthquakes occur, but recent observations indicate a relationship with the hydrological cycle at glaciers and ice sheets. The number of earthquakes that  occur on Greenland is strongly seasonally modulated, with the largest number of events occurring during the late summer months. A rapid increase in the number of earthquakes at outlet glaciers across Greenland since approximately 2000 suggests a link to large-scale climate change.    The proposed research consists of two parts: (1) a field deployment of Global Positioning System (GPS) stations on Helheim Glacier, East Greenland, to obtain direct measurements of the displacement transients associated with glacial earthquakes, the logistical costs for which will be funded separately; and (2) integrated, interdisciplinary analysis of recorded GPS, seismic, and glaciological data using state-of-the-art techniques from each field to obtain an understanding of the mechanism by which glacial earthquakes occur. Seismic analyses will provide long-wavelength estimates of the earthquake source characteristics, while the geodetic observations will provide detailed information about the timing and pattern of deformation within the glacier. A combined analysis of these datasets will result in geophysically consistent models of the deformation process, which will then be studied in the context of glaciological observations of the background glacier behavior and time-varying melting rates to evaluate the hypothesis that surface melting is linked to the generation of glacial earthquakes.     Intellectual Merit. The proposed research will lead to a greatly improved understanding of the processes controlling glacial earthquakes, a previously unknown geophysical phenomenon. It will also provide insight into modes of glacier deformation and possible connections between glacialearthquake activity and global climate change.     Broader Impacts. The results of the proposed study will be important for glaciologists and climatologists in addition to geodesists and seismologists. The understanding of glacial earthquakes developed as a result of this study will allow remote-sensing seismic data to be used as a tool in comparative glaciology and studies of global change, while also leading to improved knowledge of the response of the solid Earth to transient deformation events at or near the Earth’s surface.
Project_Title: Geodetic constraints on the mechanism of glacial earthquakes

Abstract: Small light-absorbing carbonaceous particles ("black carbon", BC) are produced by incomplete combustion in burning of fossil fuels or biomass. The particles are often carried for several days by the atmosphere before being scavenged by raindrops or snow crystals. Radiative transfer modeling and previous published measurements indicate that parts-per-billion amounts of BC can reduce snow albedo significantly, potentially affecting the Arctic climate and the stability of sea ice. BC in snow and ice has recently been identified as one of the largest uncertainties in estimates of global radiative forcing for climate change, because of inadequate knowledge of the BC concentrations. In previous work, the BC content of snow on land and sea in the western Arctic was measured in 1983-4, suggesting possible reductions of albedo of 0-4%. However, there are indications from measurements in 1998 at the SHEBA location that snow in the Arctic Ocean may now be less polluted than 20 years ago.    In this project an updated and more comprehensive survey will be undertaken, covering the eastern Arctic as well. Samples will be taken during March-May (i.e., near the time of maximum snow depth) on the Arctic Ocean, in tundra areas of Russia, Alaska, and Canada, in both wet-snow and dry-snow zones of the Greenland Ice Sheet, and on ice caps in Iceland. Glacier ice will be sampled in summer in the ablation zone of the Greenland Ice Sheet; there is evidence that its albedo is reduced by BC as well. Snow samples will be taken at several vertical levels through the snowpack. Snow samples will be collected by project personnel and also by volunteer researchers engaged in other projects at remote field camps. The snow will be melted and filtered; the filters will then be analyzed for light transmission as a function of wavelength, to separate the contributions to absorption by BC and soil-dust. The snow must be kept frozen until immediately before filtering, to avoid losses of BC to the container walls and to avoid algal growth; therefore, much of the analysis will be done near the collection sites. At one or more locations snow samples will be collected over the course of the melting season, to document the vertical redistribution of BC. BC is usually hydrophobic, so as the snow melts it may tend to concentrate at the surface, where it has a greater effect on albedo than if uniformly distributed. Spectral albedo will also be measured at some locations to relate the BC concentrations to their radiative effects. The effect of BC on the surface albedo will be estimated both regionally and seasonally, for use in climate modeling. Air sampling concurrent with snowfall events will be carried out at one or more locations, to determine the scavenging ratio, which is needed in atmospheric transport models that link emissions of aerosols to deposition in precipitation.
Place: Cambridge Bay, Cherskii, Dikson Island, DYE-2, Igloolik, Inuvik, Kangerlussuaq, Khatanga, Nar'yan-Mar, Noril'sk, Raven, Resolute, Svalbard, Tiksi, Utqiaġvik, Vorkuta, Yakutsk
Project_Title: Black carbon in Arctic snow and ice and its effect on surface albedo

Abstract: The integration of immigrants into a host society is a problem of widespread concern. This project, by graduate student Johanna Yngvason under the direction of Dr. E. Paul Durrenberger, will open up a relatively unexplored aspect of international migration by assessing the role of marriage in population flows, offering insight to any country with an influx of female labor migrants and brides from abroad, including the United States. This project will use ethnographic field methods to examine marriage and labor migration of Thai women to Iceland and will assess how these channels differentially affect integration into the Icelandic community.     Yngvason estimates from her preliminary fieldwork in August 2005 that at least half of the Thai migrant women came specifically to marry Icelanders, while the rest of the women came for labor opportunities and are kin of the marriage migrants. Yngvason will collect further data during 12 months of ethnographic work among Thai migrants in Iceland (approximately 800 individuals) using participant-observation and surveys among a random sample of 260 individuals; she will then compare outcomes between the two groups in terms of the degree of their integration into Icelandic society. The survey will complement daily interaction with the population to measure Icelandic language skills and usage, type and density of networks, choices of leisure activities and cuisine, religious institutional involvement, and activities with people in Thailand.    This study will enhance anthropology's contribution to migration studies through the ethnographic understanding of marriage and the economy as predictors of women's migration. The study will also contribute to an understanding of how people negotiate cultural differences and under what circumstances they try or do not try to do so. Iceland has no shared borders, creating an optimal situation for the documentation and observation of immigrants and their level of integration in their host society. The results of the study have implications for the formation of national policies on immigration. The project will also contribute significantly to the education of a female social scientist.
Project_Title: Doctoral Dissertation Improvement Grant: Thai Migrant Women and Relative Success of Integration in Iceland

Abstract: For Eskimo people, song and dance have long been vehicles for transmitting history, traditions, and cultural values. Today, the expressive cultures have become a way of (re)articulating ethnic identity, representing culture in political discourses, and interpreting tradition within communities. My previous field work and preliminary studies in Barrow, Alaska, suggests that dance and song combine a cultural aesthetics with abstract and embodied knowledge of the Arctic environment in a harmony of movements and sounds. Contemporary Iñupiat perceive that song and dance from the past, which portray their land, worldview, and subsistence activities, objectify their traditions and express their identity as an ethnic minority in the broader, multi-ethnic context of national and global spheres. Yup’ik people in the Southwest, on the other hand, have dramatically different history and contemporary status of indigenous dance. While Iñupiat perceive song and dance as relation to the past and strong ethnic marker in their identity, Yup’ik orientation is to the present rather than the past. These comparative situations lead the following research questions: How are endangered language preservation programs, socio economic situations, and political discourse with the dominant society connected to contemporary Eskimo understandings of tradition? While some indigenous groups use their tradition as a starting point for incorporating new styles evocative of modern culture, why do other indigenous people define their identity as emergent from old tradition? The intellectual merits of this study include gaining a better understanding of the nature and structure of Eskimo peoples’ aesthetic forms of expression, indigenous language proficiency, their traditionality, and meanings of tradition wrought by political, economic, and historical events. I hypothesize that dance performances are the key sphere where people regenerate, reinterpret, and renegotiate their traditions to themselves and to wider audiences.  Under guidance of Dr. Molly Lee, my principal investigator, and Dr. Alex King, my graduate advisor, the proposed research will be a part of my doctorial training. In the course of ethnographic research in Yup’ik and Iñupiaq communities, I will analyze the meanings of dance, song, and tradition told by indigenous people from various generations. In the current anthropological literature of song and dance, few address issues of relationships between knowledge of expressive cultures, knowledge systems, and perception of the environment. No one has focused on how language endangerment is related to the creation of ritual language through traditional songs. By comparing Yup’ik and Iñupiaq communities which vary in language maintenance, colonial histories, and economic development, this project will contribute to anthropological theory in several ways: 1) role of dance and song as pragmatic, material activities; 2) relationship between song and language endangerment; and 3) tradition defined by indigenous peoples and asymmetrical power relationships. The broader impacts of the study include contributions to documentation and analysis of contemporary indigenous dance and song focusing on their languages and ecological knowledge, which will be useful for the host communities to establish criteria for re-examing their historical and cultural pasts and developing further community-based programs. In addition to a Ph.D. dissertation, journal articles and presentation in local and academic meetings, I plan to work with community members, local educators, and personnel in regional heritage centers to design programs to educate younger people integrating their languages and expressive cultures.
Project_Title: Dissertation Research: Dance, Language, and Power among the Yup’iks and the Inupiat in Alaska

Abstract: Ancient ice is melting as a result of climate change in high latitude regions. The character and cultural use of poorly-known features of perennial ice, called “ice patches,” are the focus of this research. Rare and well preserved organic artifacts, including clothing, baskets, and tools are melting from glaciers and ice patches around the world. Radiocarbon dating demonstrates that these specimens have been frozen for thousands of years, providing a unique opportunity to investigate the role of these features in high latitude human adaptations. Four locales identified by preliminary research in Alaska’s Wrangell St. Elias National Park and Preserve (WRST) (NSF OPP #0222490) will be studied to understand the archeology of ice patches. The primary research objectives employ a cultural ecological approach to: 1) document and interpret the role of ice patches in early high latitude human adaptations, 2) evaluate and interpret their role in high latitude cultural development, 3) define the composition, character, and projected longevity of ice patches from a geoarcheological perspective, and 4) develop methods to identify possible fossil ice patches so that these sites can be recognized after the ice has melted. A long term interdisciplinary research project is necessary to accomplish these goals. This interdisciplinary research frontier presents new and unique scientific challenges. It will expand the emerging field of icefield archeology and develop original levels of integrated cooperative science. The research will produce observations and expand concepts that that may have broad application in other high latitude/altitude regions of the world. It will contribute unique and essential baseline data and knowledge about the prehistory and paleoecology of a poorly known region, expand the discipline of geoarcheology, and provide a fresh opportunity to evaluate the concept that polar environments are “barometers” of climate, environmental, and cultural change. It will enhance community archeology and regional cultural pride by working with Athapaskan people (Ahtna) and other community members to integrate archeology, local knowledge, and public education.  This research will: 1) educate and excite the public, educators, planners, managers, and funders about climate change and the need to locate, collect and preserve rare organic remains before they are lost forever; 2) continue to revise and contribute to the larger body of anthropological knowledge and human cultural ecology. The research provides opportunities for Native Americans, an under represented group in science education, to participate in and contribute to science. Artifacts resulting from this project will contribute to a regional museum/cultural center in the Copper River region planned jointly by the Ahtna Heratige Foundation and the National Park Service. This facility will provide broad cultural and educational opportunities to local residents and to thousands of tourists who visit the area annually. This research coincides with International Polar Year (IPY) - 4 (2007-9) and will support and enhance its goals and themes.
Place: Wrangell-Saint Elias National Park and Preserve
Project_Title: Ice Patch Archaeology

Abstract: This radiocarbon dating project is a collaborative of 0614840 (Pigati, University of Arizona, LEAD), 0614647 (Rech, Miami University) and 0614903 (Nekola, University of New Mexico).    Terrestrial gastropods are one of the most successful animal groups on Earth. They occupy and thrive in incredibly diverse habitats, ranging from marshes and grasslands to upland forests and arctic tundra. Their distribution in the fossil record is equally diverse. Gastropod shells are commonly found in lake, wetland, alluvial, loess, and glacial deposits, as well as in sediments at archeological sites worldwide. Yet despite their widespread occurrence in the fossil record and the fact that they contain ~12% by weight carbon, gastropod shells are usually avoided for 14C dating because many taxa incorporate 14C-deficient (or "dead") carbon from limestone when building their shells. Geochronologists refer to this as the "Limestone Problem" because the amount of dead carbon incorporated in gastropod shells is variable at all taxonomic levels and can cause 14C ages to be up to 3,000 years too old. However, PIs preliminary results from the American Southwest suggest that some small (maximum body dimension <10 mm) gastropods avoid limestone even when it is readily available. Moreover, these same taxa appear to remain closed systems with respect to carbon over geologic timescales in arid environments. Thus, at least in dry conditions, some small terrestrial gastropod shells may in fact provide reliable 14C ages. The primary research objective of this study is to clearly identify gastropod taxa that are capable of consistently yielding reliable 14C ages, regardless of local lithology, environmental conditions, climate, or ecological habitat. To this end, PIs will conduct a systematic analysis of the 14C content of a suite of modern and fossil terrestrial gastropods that are endemic to North America. They have targeted more than 30 extant species that will be used to answer the following research questions: (1) do individuals of a specific taxon always avoid limestone when building their shells, and (2) if so, do their shells remain closed systems over time regardless of local environmental conditions? The wide taxonomic, ecological, and taphonomic scope of this study will allow PIs to determine what types of gastropod shells can be used to reliably date Quaternary sediments. Moreover, this approach will help other investigators identify additional target species, including those outside North America, by providing a priori guidelines for the identification of taxa that use only metabolically-generated carbon in shell construction and that will hence provide accurate 14C ages.
Project_Title: Collaborative research: Radiocarbon dating of North American terrestrial gastropod shells

Abstract: This award supports dissertation research on the salmon industry in Bristol Bay, Alaska.  An ethnographic study of fishing practice and policymaking, the project examines how large-scale processes of contemporary economic restructuring both affect and are potentially renegotiated by workers’ lived experience and locally specific modes of valuation.  Like many other resource industries worldwide, the Alaskan salmon industry has witnessed volatile economic shifts in recent years as a result of the broad market transformations associated with globalization.  Yet unlike other sites of global industrial restructuring, Bristol Bay fishing is both heavily regulated by the state and subject to at least nominal control by industry participants themselves.  For this reason, Bristol Bay provides an ideal context to ask how heterogeneous groups of stakeholders negotiate the often contradictory demands and ideals forged by new global economic orders, local industry cultures, and tight-knit communities alike:  Do workers’ designs for and responses to regulatory change serve to support, resist, or transform dominant policy paradigms?  How are divergent histories and cultural forms integrated into--or excluded from--the collective action of resource regulation?    This research will contribute to analyses of current economic globalization and restructuring as well as more general theoretical considerations of value, property, labor, and capitalism.  At the same time, it will add to the anthropology of work and the anthropology of fishing, and Northern, rural, and Alaska Native studies.  By assessing the historical, cultural, and social bases for and implications of salmon industry restructuring, this research aims to directly contribute to the construction of more effective and appropriate resource policy in Bristol Bay and beyond.
Project_Title:
Dissertation Research: Contradictions of Consolidation: Labor, Nature,
and Fishery Restructuring in Bristol Bay, Alaska

Abstract: This project will study key elements in Earth’s geodynamic and climatic systems in the polar regions using a new suite of radar sensors that will provide a novel, comprehensive imaging of the ice surface, the internal structure and ice-bed interface with unprecedented detail. The project will bring together NSF and NASA investments in advanced radar technology, the recent advancements in airborne gravity sensing emerging from the aerogeophysical industry supplemented with more standard precision airborne magnetics and high resolution ice surface mapping. The goal of the polar imaging system will be to develop an integrated, multidisciplinary system capable of resolving (1) high resolution ice surface topography using a laser altimeter (2) the details of recent accumulation of snow as recorded in the shallow layers of the ice sheet using the accumulation radar (3) the thickness of the ice sheet and the nature of the rock-ice interface using the depth sounding / SAR capable radar (4) determine the strength of the magnetic field produced by the underlying crust through measurements of the earth’s magnetic field and (5) the strength of the earth’s gravity field.    The major academic development partners in this project are the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory (LDEO) of Columbia University and the Center for Remote Sensing of Ice Sheets (CReSIS) Science and Technology Center at Kansas University. Lamont will serve as the primary coordinator of this development project while the CReSIS center will provide the radar sounders and engineering support during the test phases in Calgary and Greenland. The resulting facility will be managed jointly between LDEO and the CReSIS facility. Industrial collaborators include the Sander Geophysics and Canadian Micro Gravity systems (CMG). The program will work closely with UNAVCO for positioning requirements and support and with NCALM for implementation of the laser profiling system. Other academic partners include Elizabeth City State University and the University of Copenhagen. The USGS Crustal Imaging and Characterization Team, Denver, is also closely involved in development and implementation of this project.
Project_Title: Development of a Polar Multidisciplinary Airborne Imaging System for the International Polar Year 2007-2009

Abstract: Most indigenous populations throughout the world, the US included, have lagged behind in access to adequate health care, especially where maternal and infant care is concerned (WHO, 2005). In response, many countries formulated plans that sought to alleviate the effects of this disparity by transporting pregnant women from their villages to a central hub for delivery. Evaluations of the impact of these policies, however, have been mostly based on maternal and infant mortality rates—with little emphasis on the impact to the cultural connectedness of the community’s families (see French, 1997). Neither has the impact of the lack of continuity of care on the mother and infant in these situations been as predominant as the more-easily measured maternal or infant mortality rates (US Dept. HHS, 2005, for example).
Project_Title:
Dissertation Research Study of How Changes in Childbirth Practices
Affect Cultural Connectedness: A Comparative Analysis

Abstract: This award provides funding for students in the Department of Alaska Native and Rural Development at the University of Alaska to attend a workshop on Traditional Knowledge, Environmental Change and Development in the Arctic. The workshop, co-hosted by Ilisagvik College, the Barrow Arctic Research Consortium, and the National Park Service, provides an opportunity for students to interact with scientists, policy makers, and rural residents working on Arctic relevant issues such as: Western Science and Traditional Knowledge, Climate Change, Subsistence and Co-management, and Oil, Mineral and Gas Development and its Implications for Local Social and Cultural Development.
Project_Title: Traditional Knowledge, Environmental Change and Development in the Arctic

Abstract: For many indigenous communities in the Arctic, strong, intimate relationships with the environment are the cornerstone to their culture. Sea ice, one of the most prominent and important features of the Arctic environment, is changing due to global environmental change. Human-sea ice relationships that are deeply rooted in time, as well as identity, are being challenged. There is an urgent need to better understand the human and social dynamics surrounding Arctic sea ice change and what is at stake for coastal communities so that stakeholders at all levels, from the individual to the international, can make more informed decisions about managing societal responses to a changing Arctic environment, responses that may have far-reaching implications. To achieve this requires collaboration across disciplines, countries, cultures, and worldviews. Our project meets these requirements and brings together the needed experience to effectively achieve project goals.    Intellectual Merit: To better understand the dynamics of changes to human-sea ice relationships, we propose a comparative study in three Arctic communities (Barrow, Alaska; Clyde River, Nunavut, Canada; Qaanaaq, Greenland). In an innovative “knowledge exchange” approach, we bring together a multidisciplinary, multi-cultural team of scientists and indigenous hunters and elders. Our unique research team will to travel together to each study location in order to examine:  1. Characteristics of sea ice and its use by humans (e.g., seasonal patterns, use of specific features and zones, thickness, etc.), including the role of the human-sea ice relationship in social organization of the three communities   2. Changes in human use patterns over time (e.g., effects of modernization, effects of varying styles of governance, effects of environmental change, hunting regulations, etc.)   3. Changes to sea ice, with particular attention to the features most crucial for human uses (e.g., seasonality, shorefast ice formation, roughness, etc.)  4. Recent human responses to changes in sea ice (e.g., acquisition of new knowledge, changes in hunting patterns, changes in equipment, etc.)  5. Societal impacts from sea ice changes and human responses (e.g., reduced role for elders as old knowledge becomes less relevant, changes in harvest patterns, increased risk to travel safety and food security, greater reliance on regional government, etc.)  6. Implications for future changes, impacts, and adaptations (e.g., shifts in hunting patterns, reliance on new technology, changes in regulatory regimes, effects on social organization, etc.)  The three communities offer differences in geography, political organization, and recent history, along with similarities of culture and dependence on marine mammals. Comparisons across time and space, and of indigenous knowledge and science, offer rich possibilities for analysis and insight. For each of our three communities, we will examine human uses of sea ice in recent decades and the environmental and societal conditions that have influenced specific uses and changes. For example: the use of snow machines instead of dog teams; thinning ice and changing weather patterns; and regulations governing hunting (e.g. bowhead whale in Alaska and Nunavut).
Project_Title: DHB: The Dynamics of Human-Sea Ice Relationships: Comparing Changing Environments in Alaska, Nunavut and Greenland

Abstract: The auroras are characterized not only be a variety of active optical emissions, but by a wide variety of radio emissions as well. The relationship between different optical features and different radio features, however, is poorly understood. Wave phenomena in the auroral regions play an important role in the energy flow between the magnetosphere and the ionosphere. In order to understand the relationships between optical and radio phenomena in the auroral region it is necessary to monitor the region with a variety of instruments. This project will utilize data from optical imaging instruments, radar backscatter from auroral features, and plasma wave, electric field, magnetic field and particle measurements from satellites crossing the auroral regions. Satellites which will be used in the study include the defense department DMSP satellites, NASA's FAST, WIND, POLAR, SAMPEX, and IMAGE satellites, and the European CLUSTER mission. A ground-based radio imaging system will be used to locate the regions producing auroral Medium Frequency (MF) radio emissions. The investigation will also contribute to studies of the timing and location of magnetic substorm onsets. The radio imaging instruments will be deployed at existing facilities in Alaska and Greenland. The data will be made available to all researchers, including those using the Alaska and Greenland facilities. The research project will also be integrated with educational activities being carried out by the collaborating institutions. In particular the educational effort at Dartmouth will include a focus toward the Dartmouth Women-in Science-Program (WISP). Students will be involved with both the engineering aspects of the new instrumentation as well as the analysis of the resulting scientific data.
Project_Title: Collaborative Research: Imaging Auroral Radio Emissions: Multitechnique Investigations Employing Optical, Radar, and Satellite Instruments.

Abstract: SCENOP will seek to identify cross-cultural regularities and differences in human responses to rapid environmental change in prehistory. By collecting and analyzing archaeological and paleo-environmental data from two widely separated but environmentally comparable circumpolar paleo-estuaries, the Yli-Ii area of Northern Finland and the Wemindji area of James Bay in Quebec, the project will provide information about how prehistoric groups created sustainable adaptive systems in response to the environmental challenges while developing historically unique sets of life-ways. SCENOP is a collaborative research project between several research centers including the Social Systems GIS laboratory of the State University of New York at Buffalo in the US (SSGIS). The aim of the U.S. research at the University at Buffalo is to develop GIS (geographical information systems) models of paleo-environmental and archaeological data within the larger objectives of SCENOP’s BOREAS project. SCENOP’s two main objectives are to determine the similarities in environmental change experienced by prehistoric inhabitants of James Bay (Old Factory Lake paleo-estuary) and Northern Finland (Yli-Ii paleo-estuary), and the nature of resultant social change. To these ends, GIS layers will be produced by integrating terrestrial models, archaeological data sets, and environmental data sets from two Arctic regions, the Yli-Ii area of Northern Finland and the Wemindji area of James Bay in Quebec. The intellectual merit for examining these two problems is the contribution to our understanding of the relationship between environmental and social change, and societal adaptive responses to climate fluctuations, which is directly relevant to global warming. In addition, the broader impact of understanding variability in regional settlement patterns, land-use, and resource exploitation throughout history will be an understanding of issues facing Nordic populations today.
Project_Title: Social change and the environment in Nordic prehistory: Evidence from Finland and northern Canada. (SCENOP)

Abstract: This Polar Postdoctoral Fellowship allows the PI to carry out a wide-ranging program in the anthropology of food among the arctic native people. The program encompasses archival research, ethnographic fieldwork in the Russian Far East, seminar participation at the Yale Institute for Social and Policy Studies, writing workshops, and a reading course, integrated within a study plan, to be carried out in the Department of Anthropology, Johns Hopkins University and at the Arctic Studies Center, Smithsonian Institution. Based on prior ethnographic fieldwork in the Bering Strait, the work promises to reintegrate northern anthropology, by identifying common webs of significance that connect this work to other disciplines and inquiries conducted outside the circumpolar North, as well as by strengthening relationships with host communities in Chukotka and Alaska.
Place: Enmelen, Lavrentiya, New Chaplino, Nome, Nunligran, Provideniya, Sireniki
Project_Title: Postdoctoral Research Fellowship

Abstract: This project is a collaboration between Woodgate, UW (0632154), and Weingartner, UAF (0631713).    The Bering Strait, a narrow (~ 85 km wide), shallow (~ 50 m deep) strait at the northern end of the Pacific, is the only ocean gateway between the Pacific and the Arctic. Although the flow through the strait is small in volume, due to its remarkable properties (high heat and freshwater content, low density, high nutrients) it has a startling strong influence, not only on the Chukchi Sea and the Arctic Ocean, but also on the North Atlantic overturning circulation and possibly world climate. At a time when dramatic change, especially the retreat of sea ice, is observed in the Bering and Chukchi seas and the Arctic, we have measured significant increases of Bering Strait fluxes of volume, freshwater and heat, the heat flux in 2004 being the maximum recorded in the last 15 years.      This research, also in collaboration with Russian, Canadian and Japanese colleagues, is an observationally focused study of the entire Bering Strait region, consisting of a high resolution mooring array, deployed from 2007-2009, covering the two channels of the strait and one “climate” site to the north of the strait, supported by annual CTD surveys and mooring servicing, satellite data and theoretical and modeling results.     The science objectives are:  1) to measure the velocities and water properties of the Bering Strait throughflow;  2) to understand the physical processes influencing the properties of the Bering Strait throughflow, with special focus on mechanisms driving change, and impacts on the Arctic Ocean;  3) to quantify oceanic fluxes of volume, freshwater, heat, nutrients and chlorophyll biomass through the strait;  4) to design an optimum monitoring system for oceanic fluxes through the Bering Strait.    Relevance to IPY: The Bering Strait is recognized as a key ocean gateway by the Arctic Observing Network plans of SEARCH (Study of Environmental Arctic Change), the National Academies report, and international IPY projects. Our proposed work is the lead of an international (US-Russian-Canadian-Japanese) IPY project, built on our ICSU endorsed IPY proposal for the Bering Strait. The work is also a key element of the IPY projects COME (Canada Ocean Monitoring Experiment - studying linkages among the subarctic and arctic waters around Canada), “66N” (Ocean transports across 66ºN from satellite altimetry, numerical models and in situ observations), and iAOOS (international Arctic Ocean Observing System). Our approach includes a pulse of activity in the IPY years, a legacy of data and infrastructure, training the next generation of scientists, and outreach to the public.
Project_Title: IPY: COLLABORATIVE RESEARCH: The Pacific Gateway to the Arctic-Quantifying and Understanding Bering Strait Oceanic Fluxes

Abstract: This grant will work in conjunction with multiple national and international IPY projects to include: the Russian Central Arctic Ocean Complex Study (CAOCS); the Canadian Ocean Monitoring Experiment (COME) and the Canadian Arctic Margin Experiment (CAME) projects; the European Union’s Developing Arctic Modeling and Observing Capabilities of Long-term Environmental Studies (DAMOCLES) project; the Russian Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute (AARI); and the UK Arctic Synoptic Basin-wide Oceanography (ASBO) project. The group will use the facilities at the North Pole Environmental Observatory (NPEO) and be a part of the International Arctic Buoy Program (IABP).    The research expands ongoing efforts to develop, test and field a set of Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) Ice-Tethered Profilers (ITPs): autonomous instruments that return high-vertical-resolution measurements of upper ~800 m ocean temperature, salinity, and dissolved oxygen beneath sea ice during all seasons at better than daily temporal resolution. The WHOI ITPs will repeatedly sample the upper ocean water properties beneath the permanently ice-covered Arctic for up to a 3-year period (expected lifetime of an average multi-year ice floe) and telemeter those data to shore in near-real time. Data returned from these instruments will support studies of ocean processes, facilitate numerical model initialization and validation, and stimulate general interest in Arctic science issues. Research and understanding that builds on these observations will lead to better appreciation of the Arctic’s role in the earth’s climate system.
Place: Beaufort Sea, Canada Basin, North Pole
Project_Title: IPY: Towards an Arctic Observing Network: An array of Ice-Tethered Profilers to sample the upper ocean water properties during the International Polar Year

Abstract: IPY Relevance: International Polar Year presents an extraordinary opportunity to educate students and the public about science at the icy ends of the Earth. The goal of this proposal is to apply collaborative multimedia approaches to bring polar research expeditions to the general public and the classroom. These include:     • Expedition 1: “Towards an Arctic Observing Network: An array of Ice-Tethered Profilers to sample the upper ocean water properties during the International Polar Year” (J. Toole et al, grant #0631951)    • Expedition 2: “Hydrothermal Processes on the Gakkel Ridge” (PIs: R. Reves-Sohn et al, grant #0425838.)    • Expedition 3: Antarctica project TBD.    • Expedition 4: “Behavior of supraglacial lakes and their role in outlet glacier dynamics and mass balance of the Greenland Ice Sheet” (PIs: S. Das et al grant #0520077).    A science writer and a professional photographer will join each expedition and file dispatches for a daily Webcast. The writer will also coordinate real-time phone patches from PIs in the field to audiences at the Museum of Science, Boston, the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Liberty Science Center, Carnegie Museum of Natural History, Houston Museum of Natural Science, The Field Museum, the Birch Aquarium, the Pacific Science Center, National Public Radio stations, and to student “reporters” writing for Scholastic Online. In addition to building and promoting an online experience, a museum exhibit will be developed at the WHOI Exhibit Center highlighting research results and instruments. Components of this exhibit will travel to partner museums in Boston and Washington, D.C.
Place: Gakkel Ridge, Ilulissat, Kangerlussuaq, Lake 1, Lake 2
Project_Title:
IPY: Collaborative Research: Live from the Poles; A Multimedia
Educational Experience

Abstract: This research is part of an international collaborative effort involving scientists from several institutions. The funds support participation of U.S. scientists from the Universities of Colorado and Kansas in the NEEM (North Eemian Ice Core) project for the International Polar Year (IPY). NEEM aims to drill new deep ice core in northern Greenland to address past and future environments and climates. The researchers expect to obtain a climate record for the last interglacial period, the Eemian, and for some of the ice age preceding that (called Saale in Europe, and Illinoian in the US). In round terms, the researchers intend to collect ice cores recording climate history reaching back 150,000 years.     Climate records from the Eemian period are of particular interest to scientists because, with temperatures 3 –5 degrees warmer and sea levels 3-5 meters higher than today, the Eemian makes an interesting analog for climate in the near future. Using core and radar mapping data, researchers will be able to estimate the size of the Greenland ice sheet when sea level was many meters higher than today. Further, the core may reveal if abrupt climate change occurred in the Eemian period, which could in turn offer better future predictive power for abrupt climate shifts and add to growing knowledge about how alterations of climate and the environment by humans fit within the context of natural climate change.     NEEM is an international effort, led by the glaciology group at the University of Copenhagen. In addition to the United States, contributions also come from the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden, France, the U.K., South Korea, China, Japan, Canada, Iceland, Germany, and Switzerland.
Project_Title: IPY: Collaborative Research: The NEEM Deep Ice Core

Abstract: In a rapidly changing Arctic, the shrinking and thinning sea-ice cover plays an important role as indicator and agent of environmental change. A dramatic shrinking of the perennial ice cover has greatly increased the extent and hence importance of the Arctic seasonal ice zone (SIZ). The SIZ is predicted to occupy much of the Arctic by mid- to late century, but data are sorely lacking to aid in tracking, understanding and predicting change over this important component of the Arctic cryosphere.    This interdisciplinary project implements an integrated program for observing seasonal ice in the context of sweeping environmental, (geo)political and socio-economic change in the North. In addition to sampling of sea-ice state variables, the observation-system design is guided by the concept of sea-ice system services (SISS). By assessing the nature and extent of SISS, an integrated observation network can be built that will lead to prediction of key trends in a changing Arctic in a way that provides maximum benefit for the broadest range of affected interests.    The project’s overarching scientific goal is to track intertwined changes and selected important impacts in a rapidly evolving Seasonal Ice Zone (SIZ) in order to improve our understanding and predictions of the Arctic sea-ice cover over the course of the century.    The project will establish a network of researchers, Arctic residents, different institutions with needs for sea-ice information, and other stakeholders. It will deliver infrastructure and an integrated sea-ice data set, leaving a legacy that allows for continued, long-term observations beyond the IPY “test bed.”   Specific objectives are to:  (1) Identify a set of sea-ice variables that helps answer the key scientific questions and is of greatest value to the stakeholder communities while being operationally tractable.   (2) Provide a framework for assessing sea-ice observations during IPY in the context of large-scale spatial and temporal variability.  (3) Create a protocol for integrated sea ice observations. Drawing on results from aims #1 and 2, an observation protocol will be developed to guide ice observations during the IPY and beyond.  (4) Complete a series of networked, integrated pan-Arctic SIZ observations, and disseminate the data to relevant user and stakeholder groups through appropriate archival and distribution centers. This effort will involve partners from six nations and draw on existing resources and programs already in place.  (5) Analyze observations in a dialog with potential users, aimed at refining the observation strategy to create a legacy network for the post-IPY phase. As data from the first season are available, a dialog with representatives of key user groups will take place, aimed at improving the scope and mode of data collection and dissemination. At the end of the project, based on the data sets assembled, an IPY legacy observing network that will rely on a combination of autonomous sensors, local observers and continuing operational and scientific efforts will be outlined.
Project_Title: IPY: Collaborative Research on the State of the Arctic Sea Ice Cover: An Integrated Seasonal Ice Zone Observing Network (SIZONET)

Abstract: This grant, a collaboration between 0632131 (Sturm, CRREL, LEAD), 0632160 (Kane, UAF) and 0632133 (Liston, CSU), will provide a prototype international network where instruments will measure precipitation and snow on the ground concurrently, thereby improving the ability to monitor both of these better. At 5 arctic sites (all identified as key locations in a pan-arctic monitoring network), the field teams will augment existing meteorological and snow measuring instrumentation with solid-state snow pillows, heated plate precipitation sensors, snow fences (to capture the wind-blown flux), and eddy correlation towers for computation of sublimation. The team will conduct ground surveys of snow cover depth, water equivalent, and other properties using tools that allow rapid collection of extensive data several times a year. These will be augmented with aerial photography and airborne remote sensing from inexpensive platforms (kites and UAVs) to visualize drift and deposition patterns. The combined suite of instruments and measurements is designed to allow the researchers to close the winter water balance at each site, for the first time balancing the precipitation with measured accumulation.    This project will substantially advance understanding of how best to monitor arctic precipitation and will result in better knowledge of the spatial and historic trends in arctic winter precipitation and snow cover. Within the U.S., this understanding will directly benefit the National Resource Conservation Service (NRCS), one of the prime agencies charged with monitoring precipitation and snow cover. Similarly, the results of the project will have impact in Canada and Russia, where these agencies are charged with arctic precipitation monitoring (Environment Canada and Roshydromet). Collectively, the group of researchers will form an international arctic snow cover and winter precipitation group that can address the challenges of producing high quality assessments of arctic winter weather trends together.     Specifically, as result of the work, this group will a) identify the environmental conditions under which instruments become unreliable and learn how to flag these in the operational records, and b) identify favorable pairings of instruments that facilitate quality checking and which, when used in tandem, produce better data from both instruments. In addition, the project will contribute to the education of a graduate student, and will have direct impact on the general public through the publication of an English-Inupiat glossary of snow terms that will be used in the North Slope Borough School District Bilingual Education Program.
